name: Ubud
tagline: Bali's cultural and spiritual heart, ringed by rice terraces and known worldwide for yoga, arts and a slower pace than the coast.
highlight: Watching the Tegalalang rice terraces catch the late-afternoon light, their stepped green tiers dropping away down the valley.
shortDescription: Bali's inland cultural centre, surrounded by rice terraces, ancient temples and a deep-rooted arts and wellness scene.
metaDescription: An Ubud travel guide: the Tegalalang Rice Terraces, the Monkey Forest, Ubud Palace, yoga, food and how to plan a visit to Bali's cultural heart.
nearestAirport: Ngurah Rai International (DPS), about 1 hour away
knownFor: Rice terraces, yoga retreats, Balinese arts and temples
goodFor: Culture, wellness, a slower pace inland from the coast

image.file: File:Tegalalang Rice Terrace - Subak Ceking on Bali 15.jpg
image.alt: The stepped green tiers of the Tegalalang Rice Terraces near Ubud, Bali

intro: Ubud is Bali's cultural and spiritual centre, an inland town of rice terraces, ancient temples and a long-standing arts scene that has drawn visitors seeking something more reflective than the island's beach resorts since well before 'Eat, Pray, Love' put it on the wider map.

The town itself is compact and walkable, but its real draw spreads into the surrounding countryside — the stepped green tiers of the Tegalalang Rice Terraces, sacred forests thick with monkeys and moss-covered stone, and villages still organised around the same Hindu temple and irrigation traditions that have shaped Balinese life for centuries.

Ubud has also become a global centre for yoga and wellness retreats, but it hasn't lost its working character in the process — rice farmers, temple ceremonies and daily offerings are still very much part of the town's actual rhythm, not just its marketing.

whyVisit.intro: Ubud's case rests on a genuine depth of culture and nature packed into a compact, walkable town.

points.title: The Tegalalang Rice Terraces are iconic for a reason
points.text: Stepped, hand-carved paddies cascading down a valley, still actively farmed using Bali's traditional subak irrigation system.

points.title: It's Bali's deepest cultural centre
points.text: Temples, dance performances, traditional painting and woodcarving are all still active local traditions here, not just tourist shows.

points.title: The wellness scene is well established
points.text: Decades of yoga studios, retreats and healers have made Ubud a genuine global centre for the practice, not a recent trend.

points.title: It's a peaceful, greener alternative to the coast
points.text: Cooler, quieter and slower-paced than Bali's beach towns, surrounded by rice fields rather than surf breaks.

points.title: It works well as a base for wider exploration
points.text: Central enough to reach much of southern and central Bali on manageable day trips.

attractionsIntro: Ubud's essential sights mix its famous rice terraces with significant temples and sacred sites.

attractions.name: Tegalalang Rice Terraces

image.file: File:Rice terraces on Bali - Tegalalang Rice Terrace - Indonesia 05.jpg
image.alt: The stepped rice paddies of the Tegalalang Rice Terraces

attractions.text: Bali's most photographed rice terraces, hand-carved into a steep valley and still farmed using the centuries-old subak irrigation system.
attractions.tip: Arrive early morning to beat both the crowds and the midday heat.

attractions.name: Ubud Monkey Forest

image.alt: The forested grounds of the Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary in Ubud

attractions.text: A sacred forest sanctuary home to hundreds of long-tailed macaques and three ancient temples woven through moss-covered stone.
attractions.tip: Keep all food, sunglasses and loose items zipped away — the monkeys are practised opportunists.

attractions.name: Ubud Palace

image.alt: The ornate carved gates of Ubud Palace

attractions.text: A still-functioning royal residence with elaborately carved stone gates, hosting free traditional dance performances most evenings.
attractions.tip: Arrive early for an evening dance performance — seating fills up fast.

attractions.name: Goa Gajah (Elephant Cave)

image.file: File:Goa Gajah temple, Bedulu, Bali, Indonesia, 20220824 0929 0544.jpg
image.alt: The carved stone entrance to Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave temple

attractions.text: A striking 9th-century cave temple, its entrance carved into a demon's face, with bathing pools and ruins in the surrounding gardens.
attractions.tip: The steep steps down to the rice field views behind the cave are easy to miss — don't stop at the cave alone.

attractions.name: Campuhan Ridge Walk

image.alt: The green ridge trail of the Campuhan Ridge Walk near Ubud

attractions.text: An easy, scenic ridge trail through open grassland just minutes from central Ubud, with views over two river valleys.
attractions.tip: Start at sunrise for the coolest temperatures and softest light.

attractions.name: Tegenungan Waterfall

image.alt: Tegenungan Waterfall cascading into a pool near Ubud

attractions.text: An accessible, powerful waterfall just south of Ubud, with a swimmable pool at its base and viewpoints requiring only a short walk down.
attractions.tip: The stone steps down can be slippery — sturdy sandals help more than flip-flops.

attractions.name: Pura Taman Saraswati

image.alt: Pura Taman Saraswati, a water temple with a lotus pond, in central Ubud

attractions.text: A serene water temple dedicated to the Hindu goddess of knowledge, its lotus ponds sitting right in the middle of central Ubud.
attractions.tip: Evening dance performances are held here with the temple lit up behind the stage.

thingsToDoIntro: Ubud rewards slowing down — its best experiences are cultural and restorative rather than checklist sightseeing.

thingsToDo.title: Watch a Kecak fire dance

image.alt: Performers at a traditional Kecak fire dance in Ubud

thingsToDo.text: A mesmerising performance built entirely around a chanting male chorus, telling the Ramayana story without any instruments at all.
thingsToDo.tip: Evening shows run at Ubud Palace and several other venues around town most nights.

thingsToDo.title: Take a Balinese cooking class
thingsToDo.text: A hands-on way to understand Balinese food, usually starting with a market visit before cooking a full multi-course meal.
thingsToDo.tip: Ask whether the class includes a market tour — the best ones do.

thingsToDo.title: Cycle through rice fields and villages

image.alt: Rice fields in the countryside around Ubud

thingsToDo.text: A peaceful way to see rural Bali up close, pedalling narrow paths between paddies and small family temples.
thingsToDo.tip: Early morning gives the coolest ride and the best light over the fields.

thingsToDo.title: Practice yoga at a retreat
thingsToDo.text: Ubud's long-established wellness scene means classes range from single drop-in sessions to full multi-day retreats.
thingsToDo.tip: Book popular studios a day or two ahead — well-known classes fill up fast.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the Campuhan Ridge at sunrise

image.alt: Early morning light over the Campuhan Ridge trail

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding way to start the day, with cool air, soft light and far fewer people than the midday crowds.
thingsToDo.tip: The full loop takes about 1-2 hours at an easy pace.

thingsToDo.title: Browse the Ubud Art Market
thingsToDo.text: A lively covered market of woodcarvings, textiles and paintings, right in the centre of town near the palace.
thingsToDo.tip: Bargaining is expected — start well below the first asking price.

foodIntro: Ubud's food spans Balinese classics, a thriving café scene and one of Bali's best concentrations of good restaurants.

foods.name: Babi guling

image.alt: Babi guling, Balinese spit-roasted suckling pig

foods.text: Bali's famous spit-roasted suckling pig, stuffed with a dense mix of spices and served with rice and vegetables.
foods.whereToTry: Warungs around Ubud specialising in babi guling, often selling out by early afternoon.

foods.name: Sate lilit

image.alt: Sate lilit, minced Balinese satay wrapped around skewers

foods.text: A distinctive Balinese satay, minced meat and spices wrapped around lemongrass or bamboo skewers rather than threaded as cubes.

foods.name: Bebek betutu

image.alt: Bebek betutu, slow-cooked spiced Balinese duck

foods.text: A rich, slow-cooked duck stuffed with spices and wrapped in banana leaves, traditionally cooked for hours in embers.
foods.whereToTry: Ubud's well-known duck restaurants, best ordered a few hours ahead.

foods.name: Nasi campur

image.alt: A plate of nasi campur with an assortment of Balinese side dishes

foods.text: An excellent way to sample several Balinese dishes at once, rice served with a rotating mix of vegetables, meat and sambal.
foods.whereToTry: Warungs throughout Ubud, especially near the market.

foods.name: Lawar

image.alt: Lawar, a traditional Balinese mixed vegetable and meat dish

foods.text: A traditional Balinese dish of minced vegetables, coconut and meat, usually seasoned heavily with spice and lime.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional warungs around Ubud, often as part of a nasi campur plate.

foods.name: Balinese coffee

image.file: File:Sangrai Biji Kopi secara traditional di Coffee Plantation Bali.jpg
image.alt: Traditional coffee roasting at a plantation near Ubud

foods.text: Grown on the island's volcanic slopes, with plantation visits near Ubud offering tastings alongside the notably unusual kopi luwak.
foods.whereToTry: Coffee plantations just north of Ubud, and cafés throughout town.

accommodation.intro: Ubud's accommodation ranges from simple guesthouses to some of Bali's most celebrated luxury resorts.

areas.name: Central Ubud
areas.bestFor: Walking to the palace, market and main sights
areas.text: The most convenient base, though also the busiest and most built-up part of town.

areas.name: Campuhan and the rice field edges
areas.bestFor: A quieter stay with rice field or valley views
areas.text: Still a short walk or scooter ride from central Ubud, with a noticeably calmer feel.

gettingThere.intro: Ubud is reached by road from anywhere else on Bali, with no airport of its own.

options.mode: Private car or hotel transfer from the airport
options.text: About 1-1.5 hours from Ngurah Rai International, depending on traffic.
options.detail: Most hotels can arrange a transfer, or book one ahead through a driver app.

options.text: Available for airport transfers, though pickup zones can be restricted near the terminal.
options.detail: Often cheaper than a pre-booked hotel transfer.

options.text: A budget-friendly option connecting Ubud to other parts of Bali.
options.detail: Slower than a private car, with multiple stops along the way.

gettingAround.intro: Central Ubud is walkable, though a scooter or driver helps for the surrounding sights.

options.text: Covers the palace, market, Monkey Forest and central temples easily.
options.detail: Central Ubud's main sights sit within about a 15-20 minute walk of each other.

options.text: The most flexible way to reach Tegalalang, Tegenungan and Goa Gajah.
options.detail: An international driving permit is required and increasingly enforced.

options.text: Affordable and popular for visitors who'd rather not navigate Bali's traffic themselves.
options.detail: Typically booked through a hotel or driver app for a fixed daily rate.

bestTime.headline: April to October for the driest, most comfortable weather
bestTime.summary: Ubud is pleasant year-round thanks to its inland elevation, though the dry season makes exploring outdoor sights noticeably easier.

seasons.text: The most reliable weather for rice terrace walks and outdoor exploring, and also the busiest season.
Good weather odds with thinner crowds than the July–August peak.
Still workable, with short, heavy afternoon downpours rather than constant rain, and lush, vivid green rice terraces.
The busiest and most expensive time to visit, worth booking well ahead for.

bestTime.avoid: Nothing strongly — Ubud's inland climate stays comfortable and workable year-round, wet season included.

itinerary.title: Two days in Ubud
itinerary.intro: Built around the rice terraces and temples on day one, culture and wellness on day two.

days.title: Rice terraces and temples
days.summary: Tegalalang, Goa Gajah and central Ubud's temples.
days.morning: The Tegalalang Rice Terraces, arriving early.
days.afternoon: Goa Gajah and Pura Taman Saraswati.
days.evening: A Kecak fire dance performance at Ubud Palace.

days.title: Culture and wellness
days.summary: The Monkey Forest, a cooking class and a spa evening.
days.evening: A spa treatment or a quiet dinner in central Ubud.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make an Ubud stay noticeably smoother.
tips: Dress modestly at temples — a sarong is often required and usually available to rent at the entrance.
Keep loose items zipped away at the Monkey Forest — the macaques are skilled opportunists.
Book well-known yoga classes and cooking classes a day or two ahead.
Carry small rupiah notes — many warungs and market stalls don't take cards.
Arrive at Tegalalang early to avoid both the crowds and the heat.
Negotiate a private driver's day rate upfront, before setting out.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Ubud?
faq.a: Two to four days covers the main sights and a wellness activity or two at a relaxed pace.

faq.q: Is Ubud worth visiting if I've already seen Bali's beaches?
faq.a: Yes — Ubud offers a distinctly different, more cultural and inland side of Bali that the coastal towns don't.

faq.q: How far is Ubud from the airport?
faq.a: About 1 to 1.5 hours by car, depending on traffic, with no airport of its own.

faq.q: Is the Ubud Monkey Forest safe to visit?
faq.a: Yes, with sensible precautions — keep food and loose items secured, and don't make direct prolonged eye contact with the macaques.

faq.q: Do I need a scooter in Ubud?
faq.a: Not essential — central Ubud is walkable, and a driver or scooter rental covers the outlying sights well.

faq.q: Is Ubud good for a yoga retreat?
faq.a: Yes, one of the world's best-known yoga destinations, with decades of established studios and retreats to choose from.
